name: Avoid Rainbow Cycles
description: You are given $$$m$$$ sets of integers $$$A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_m$$$; elements of these sets are integers between $$$1$$$ and $$$n$$$, inclusive. There are two arrays of positive integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m$$$ and $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$$$. In one operation you can delete an element $$$j$$$ from the set $$$A_i$$$ and pay $$$a_i + b_j$$$ coins for that. You can make several (maybe none) operations (some sets can become empty). After that, you will make an edge-colored undirected graph consisting of $$$n$$$ vertices. For each set $$$A_i$$$ you will add an edge $$$(x, y)$$$ with color $$$i$$$ for all $$$x, y \in A_i$$$ and $$$x \lt y$$$. Some pairs of vertices can be connected with more than one edge, but such edges have different colors. You call a cycle $$$i_1 \to e_1 \to i_2 \to e_2 \to \ldots \to i_k \to e_k \to i_1$$$ ($$$e_j$$$ is some edge connecting vertices $$$i_j$$$ and $$$i_{j+1}$$$ in this graph) rainbow if all edges on it have different colors. Find the minimum number of coins you should pay to get a graph without rainbow cycles.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$m$$$ and $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq m, n \leq 10^5$$$), the number of sets and the number of vertices in the graph. The second line contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m$$$ ($$$1 \leq a_i \leq 10^9$$$). The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$$$ ($$$1 \leq b_i \leq 10^9$$$). In the each of the next of $$$m$$$ lines there are descriptions of sets. In the $$$i$$$-th line the first integer $$$s_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq s_i \leq n$$$) is equal to the size of $$$A_i$$$. Then $$$s_i$$$ integers follow: the elements of the set $$$A_i$$$. These integers are from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ and distinct. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$s_i$$$ for all $$$1 \leq i \leq m$$$ does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: Print one integer: the minimum number of coins you should pay for operations to avoid rainbow cycles in the obtained graph.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1408E — Avoid Rainbow Cycles [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
